summary:
Seoul stands under the national framework of South Korea. National rules on criminal law, identity documents, military service and legal gender recognition are carried by the country record; what follows is specific to Seoul.

On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, with presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the government's appeal in a damages action brought by a transgender plaintiff identified as A, and the judgment became final when neither side appealed further. The court awarded 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed. It held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person in the middle of legal transition to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, and that the right to use restrooms comfortably is a fundamental and universal human right.

The ruling addresses police conduct rather than venue policy. It establishes that advice of this kind from an officer is unlawful in Seoul. It does not by itself require any particular venue, school or business to admit a trans person to a given restroom.
tangentialFactors: A 2021 ruling by the Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court, outside Seoul, awarded 7 million won in damages against an academy that barred a transgender student from using its restrooms. That award is more than twenty times the sum ordered in the Seoul case, and the two decisions are the documented instances in which restroom exclusion has been litigated as a damages claim.
localsOnly: A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents, cited in the coverage of the Seoul case, found that 41% used restrooms designated for another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. The figures are national aggregates; no Seoul-only breakdown was published.
outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is determined by national courts. The sources identify no rule or practice specific to Seoul on changing a gender marker, and that layer is carried by the country record.

Whether police, schools or private venues in Seoul have altered restroom practice since the July 2024 judgment is not documented in the sources.
